also_called: LLM Evaluations, Benchmarks, and Grounded Testing
one_liner: A benchmark is a fixed test with a score; it helps only if you know who ran it, what it measured, and whether it resembles your task.

steps.title: A set of test questions is chosen
steps.text: Evaluators curate a standardized suite of prompts (such as math puzzles, coding challenges, or reading comprehension passages).

stage_state.description: Folder of exam questions with fixed target answers.

steps.title: The model runs across the test set
steps.text: The language model generates answers for every question under specific prompt templates and temperature parameters.

stage_state.description: Automated runner executing queries against candidate models.

steps.title: Answers are graded against a standard
steps.text: Responses are scored automatically (using code execution, regex matching, or another model acting as a judge).

stage_state.description: Checkmarks and point tallies compiling into a summary percentage.

steps.title: Ask the four critical evaluation questions
steps.text: Before trusting a high score, check: Who conducted the test? Compared to what baseline? Under what prompt conditions? Does this test mirror what you actually need to do?

stage_state.description: Four-point checklist examining methodology and relevance.

analogy.text: Think of it like a standardized high school driving test. Scoring high on a closed parking-lot obstacle course shows the driver learned vehicle controls, but it does not tell you how they react in a sudden blizzard on an unfamiliar mountain highway.
analogy.breaks: There are hundreds of competing tests with conflicting rules, and test questions can accidentally leak into public web archives where models memorize them during pretraining (benchmark contamination).

myth.claim: A model that scores 95 percent on a famous benchmark will work well for my company's specific job.
myth.reality: Benchmark tasks rarely reflect your exact vocabulary, document formats, or edge cases. A model with a lower generic score can outperform a hyped model on your tailored domain tasks.

seen_in: Tech company launch keynotes claiming new world records
Public leaderboards (such as LMSYS Chatbot Arena or Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard)
Product marketing comparisons claiming superior reasoning capability

persona_examples.student: Choosing which free AI tool helps you study by testing each on five sample problems from your actual syllabus.
persona_examples.teacher: Evaluating an automated essay feedback tool on five previously graded papers to check if its suggestions match your standards.
persona_examples.entrepreneur: Testing customer response quality across 20 common customer inquiries before purchasing a team subscription.
persona_examples.engineer_office: Building a regression test suite that runs every week to ensure prompt updates do not degrade system reliability.

quiz.question: When a headline claims a new model achieved 98 percent on a coding test, what should you ask first?
options: Which font style did the company use in the blog post?
What was tested, under what conditions, and does that test reflect the programming tasks I do?
How many stock options did the engineers receive?
Can the model replace all human programmers immediately?
quiz.explanation: Understanding what was measured and whether test questions resemble your practical workflow is essential before trusting any metric.

quiz.question: What is benchmark contamination?
options: A computer virus affecting data center hardware
When the exact questions from a test suite are present in the model's training data, allowing it to memorize answers rather than reason
Spilling water on the computer servers
Using a test with too many difficult math problems
quiz.explanation: Contamination occurs when test questions leak into the pretraining text corpus, artificially inflating performance scores.

quiz.question: What does the metric pass@1 mean on a coding benchmark?
options: The model must attempt the problem 100 times before succeeding
The percentage of problems the model solves correctly on its very first generated attempt
Only one person in the world passed the exam
The model achieved a grade of 1 out of 10
quiz.explanation: pass@1 measures first-try accuracy without giving the model multiple opportunities to retry or debug.

explain_back.prompt: Complete this sentence to prove you understand:
explain_back.template: Before I believe an AI benchmark score, I check who ran the test, what baseline was used, and whether the questions match my actual task.

bullets: Rigorous evaluation requires held-out private test splits with canary strings to prevent training data contamination.
Human preference rankings (such as Bradley-Terry paired comparisons and Elo ratings) capture nuanced conversational satisfaction.
LLM-as-a-judge approaches require calibration against human raters to mitigate position bias, verbosity bias, and self-enhancement bias.
Task-specific evaluation harnesses (pass@k, exact match, semantic faithfulness) provide quantifiable regression protection during prompt engineering.

code_panel.title: Minimal Prompt Evaluation Runner
code_panel.code:
# Minimal automated evaluation harness (pseudocode)
test_cases = [
    {"input": "Explain RAG in one sentence", "must_contain": ["retrieve", "document"]},
    {"input": "What is MCP?", "must_contain": ["protocol", "tool"]}
]

scores = []
for item in test_cases:
    response = llm.generate(item["input"])
    passed = all(k.lower() in response.lower() for k in item["must_contain"])
    scores.append(1.0 if passed else 0.0)

accuracy = sum(scores) / len(scores)
print(f"Pass rate: {accuracy * 100:.1f}%")
